overal.goal: TaskStore's per-task lock (`lockTask`, built on `withFileLock`) is in memory, so it only serialises writers inside one process. A task write from another process (the CLI, `boof-runner mcp --stdio --admin`, a second server) can race the server's runner: the CLI's `modify` can read a task as `pending` while the server moves it to `running/` and deletes `pending/<id>`, and the CLI's atomic write then recreates `pending/<id>`; the reconciler prefers the newer `updated` time, so the task can look pending while it runs. Make the task lock work across processes with `withProcessLock`, as the auth store and the project store do, without making the in-process path slower than it has to be. Found in the opus review of command-template-rename-safety (M3, 2026-11-02); it existed before for every task write from another process.

rules.do: Read packages/heart/src/store.ts (lockTask, save, modify, transition), packages/heart/src/process-lock.ts and how auth-store.ts and project-store.ts use withProcessLock (lock file location, stale lock takeover by dead pid) before changing code.
Write a failing test first: two processes (child processes, not just two promises) that modify and transition the same task must not lose a write or leave a task in two status directories.
Keep the lock files out of the task directories the readers list (no stray files in tasks/pending, tasks/ongoing and so on); check that `list`, the reconciler and the plan sync ignore them.
Run `npm run typecheck && npm test` and `npm run lint` before finishing.
rules.dont: Do not change public API or MCP shapes.
Do not commit secrets, data roots or build output.

versions.version: Filed from the command-template-rename-safety review (M3, 2026-11-02); not started.

TaskStore.lockTask uses withProcessLock on tasks/.locks/<id>.lock (outside the status directories, removed on release). Measured on ext4: an empty withProcessLock about 11 ms against 0.002 ms for the in-memory lock, and about 5 ms on top of a task write (7.6 ms): a few locked operations per task run. Tests: a server-like transition loop and a modify loop in two child processes lose no write and leave one file; the lock waits for a live holder and fails with a clear error, takes over a dead one, and stays out of the status directories.

Review follow-ups in the shared process lock (auth, migration, project create and task locks): the lock file holds "<pid> <boot id>" and a lock from another boot is stale, so a reboot that reuses the pid no longer wedges a task for 30 s (old pid-only files still read); an empty or unreadable lock older than 5 s is stale; no fsync for the lock file (atomicWrite sync: false); the takeover guard is removed only if it still names our pid; the timeout errors name the lock path. Measured on ext4 (200 tasks, 3 runs): an empty lock 6.7 ms before and 0.8 to 1.3 ms after; 200 modifies 2.9 to 4.0 s before, 2.0 to 2.4 s after, against 1.6 to 2.3 s with no lock at all. Re-review fixes: only real per-boot uuids (Linux /proc boot_id, macOS kern.bootsessionuuid) can override a live pid, so a process that cannot read one, or a lock with an old or legacy t: id, is judged by the pid alone; no id is derived from the clock any more (a clock step used to make live locks look stale); the empty-lock window is 30 s and the no-hard-link fallback does not fsync, so that path is empty for instants; the guard-owner removal has a test. Windows has no boot id (a stale lock plus a reused pid there is removed by hand, the error names the file).

The hierarchy lock (project/.locks/hierarchy.lock) and the epics.json lock (project/.locks/epics.lock) are pid locks too. Lock order unchanged and cycle-free across processes: hierarchy, then task, then epics; the task and epics critical sections never take the hierarchy lock. About 1 ms per acquisition. Tests with child processes: 50 epics created by two processes all survive (27 of 50 before); removing an epic with detach while another process creates tasks in it leaves no task naming it (failed 3 of 3 with the in-process hierarchy lock); timeout error names the lock.

Round 3 minors. m1: our own boot id must be a real uuid to override a live pid. m2: a stale lock is removed under the takeover guard only if it is still the same file (inode and mtime, not just the text), which closes the no-hard-link hole where a new lock is briefly empty like the old one. m3: a test pins the 30 s empty-lock window (10 s old is waited for). m4: the macOS sysctl call has a 2 s timeout. m5: docs only, plan sync sets a goal's epicId without the hierarchy lock and without an existence check, so that epic can dangle (flagged epicMissing); I did not take the lock there because plan sync holds an in-process per-plan lock and runs inside the runner's sync loop, and its dangling case is deliberately tolerated. m6: removeEpic --detach detaches 100 tasks per hold of the hierarchy lock; the pass that finds that many or fewer detaches them and removes the epic record under the same hold, so no task can join after the last scan (tests: a concurrent move gets in between batches; a task joining mid-way is never left naming the removed epic). m7: the lock path is resolved through realpath (withProcessLock, tryAcquireProcessLock, inspectProcessLock), so two spellings of one path, such as a symlinked project directory, share one lock (test: no overlap through a symlink, 3 overlaps before). m8: docs only, the model listing for run --tool (opencode's first listed model, up to 20 s, --model skips it); I did not cache because each run is its own process.

tests.strategy: A test that spawns a second node process doing transition/modify on the same task while the first does the same; assert no lost write and exactly one status directory holds the task.
